title: One Relative Phase Orders Operational Thresholds of Noisy Bell Pairs
abstract: Unlike the two-qubit entangled and CHSH-nonlocal sets, the steerable and Bell-nonlocal ones have no known general closed-form criterion. For any such operational ability whose failing states form a convex set closed under local unitaries, and for a Bell mixture with arbitrary noise, the $X$ part of the noise gives an upper bound on the definitive threshold, the Bell weight above which the mixture attains the ability. That bound is the tightest that the seven of the fifteen Pauli expectation values fixing the $X$ part can support. The same theorem shows that a state has the ability whenever its $X$ part does, so partial tomography of a state can certify its ability. When noise is of $X$ form, the mixture carries a relative phase between the noise and Bell coherences that cannot be gauged away by local unitaries, and it controls the threshold through interference. We prove a monotonicity law: the threshold is nondecreasing in this phase, whether or not a closed-form criterion for the ability exists.
summary: This paper develops a general framework to determine the operational thresholds of quantum abilities in noisy Bell pairs. It proves that these thresholds are governed by the X-part of the noise and exhibit a nondecreasing dependence on the relative phase between noise and coherence. This provides powerful tools for certifying quantum capabilities even when closed-form criteria are unknown.
main_problem: The paper determines the operational thresholds at which quantum communication abilities (like entanglement or steerability) are lost in noisy Bell pairs.
main_result: It establishes a monotonicity law showing that the ability threshold is nondecreasing with the relative phase between the noise and Bell coherences, and that the X-part of the noise provides a tight upper bound on this threshold.
method: The analysis uses bounding techniques based on the X-part of the noise and establishes monotonicity laws by analyzing the dependence of the threshold on the relative phase $\theta$.
model_or_system: The system models noisy Bell pairs described by a mixture $\rho_\lambda(\sigma) = \lambda \Phi_+ + (1 - \lambda) \sigma$, where $\sigma$ is the noise state characterized by its X-part $\sigma_X$.
key_observables: Operational thresholds ($\lambda_K$), the relative phase $\theta$, and the X-part of the noise ($\sigma_X$).
important_parameters: Bell weight $\lambda$ ($0 \le \lambda \le 1$) and the relative phase $\theta$ ($0 \le \theta \le \pi$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the operational ability's failing states form a convex set closed under local unitaries, and it relies on the X-part approximation for bounding.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the nondecreasing nature of operational thresholds (e.g., entanglement, CHSH-nonlocal) as a function of the relative phase $\theta$, showing certified intervals for these thresholds.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the X-part upper bound and the general monotonicity law for any suitable ability. It then focuses on the phase dependence, proving that the threshold increases monotonically with $\theta$, and finally applies these techniques to specific abilities like steerability.
why_interesting: The rigorous mathematical framework developed for characterizing thresholds based on phase dependence and partial tomography is highly general and applicable to understanding noise resilience in quantum communication protocols.
